utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, and to you Mrs. Dosen, good afternoon. May I remind you of the affirmation you made at the beginning of your evidence, which still applies. Now Mr. Vasic has some questions for you on behalf of one of the accused men. Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon to all of those present in the courtroom and good afternoon to Mrs. Dosen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Before I begin my cross-examination, I wanted to ask you the following: Since we both speak the same language, please pause between question and answer for the sake of the interpreters so that both the question and the answer could be interpreted fully and so that everyone in the courtroom could understand what we are talking about. Yesterday when my colleague Prosecutor was examining you, you said that your first husband was a JNA officer. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You had two children, a daughter and a son?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You separated from your husband in 1974?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: After the divorce, did the children stay living with you or with the husband?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: With me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In 1975 you married Mr. Martin Dosen. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: He also had two children from his first marriage; a son and daughter, born in 1972 and 1973?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did his children live with you after you married Mr. Dosen?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they lived with their mother, Marija Bozanovic, but over the weekend they would come to see us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In 1977 your daughter Tanja was born?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: At that time you lived in Mose Pijade Street. Could you please tell us what part of Vukovar that is?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To try to make it clearer, it is close to the Nama department store and the Castle Eltz, that is between the castle and the department store. Now it no longer exists.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Since it was a rather large house, did any of Martin Dosen's brothers or sisters reside with you or did you live there alone as a single family unit?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was just our immediate family.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: After you stopped working at Borovo, at a certain point you opened a fish restaurant together with your husband under the name of Martina. Could you please tell us where it was located?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was on an island across the river from the city of Vukovar. The island's name was Mala Ada.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said that your husband used to be a professional fisherman. Could you tell us what was his occupation before that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Like myself, he was an employee of the Borovo company. We both quit our jobs and became private entrepreneurs.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Your husband used to be an athlete as well when he was young. Could you tell us what sport he practiced?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He used to be a boxer and he boxed for the local club, Borovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us whether your husband used to know Zeljko Raznjatovic, aka Arkan?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he knew Zeljko. I guess it was through their gambling habits, as far as my husband told me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Pardon me, but I need to ask you this question. Did your husband ever commit any illegal acts?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, when he was still a minor.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that your husband was a member of the HDZ and that he supported their policies as expressed by the party back in 1990. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what he told me, and it was his decision, although I can't tell you exactly what he agreed to or with and not. I can only speak for myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you told us you were not a member of the HDZ, that's why I won't inquire any further, but I will move to another topic. Were Martin Dosen's brothers members of the HDZ as well?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were members of the Yugoslav party.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you or your husband know Mr. Tomislav Mercep at the time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In his activities inside the party, did your husband cooperate with Mr. Mercep?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't be certain, I don't know. I believe so, but I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that your husband was not only a member of the party, but he also supported it financially through donations?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did your husband, together with Mr. Mercep, participate in the purchase of 700 [Realtime transcript read in error "200"] Kalashnikovs for HDZ members?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, I can't offer any help on that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: My apologies, a correction for the transcript, page 4, line 14, it states 200 Kalashnikovs whereas the correct number is 700. Thank you. As far as I understood, you said you didn't know whether he participated in that or not. But do you know whether Mr. Mercep indeed purchased 700 Kalashnikovs for HDZ members?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My husband may have known, but I wasn't privy to that, and I wasn't a participant of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you give a statement to the investigators of the OTP on the 22nd of August, 1995? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that you told the investigator that the local HDZ purchased around 700 Kalashnikovs in August 1991?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I said that I heard that people were saying that Martin was one of the donors in the purchase of the weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did your husband tell you anything about the spring of 1991 and the forming of voluntary units of the HDZ headed by Mr. Mercep?

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In all honesty --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could you please pause, please, Mrs. Dosen. Yes, Mrs. Tuma.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt here, but going back to the OTP statement and by the reference of this specific sentence, what the Defence counsel is referring back to in the OTP statement, and that is the last paragraph and the last sentence, and that is that the local HDZ bought about 700 Kalashnikovs, rifles. But in the transcripts here there are another wording of that, I think. Wasn't it so? "I heard that people were saying that Martin" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mrs. Tuma.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Sorry. "I heard that people were saying that Martin was one of the donors in the purchase of the weapons." So there is a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That is what the witness said. But I think you may not have accurately quoted the statement, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: That's my point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I quoted the statement exactly, and I didn't inquire anything about the donation from the witness, she said that herself. And I believe she herself had mentioned that Martin was one of the donors. She confirmed today that she has heard of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: She has said that she doesn't know whether he was a contributor. She agrees that she told the OTP that she had heard that he was. I think that's where we've reached. Thank you. Yes, Mrs. Tuma.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: No further comments, so thank you. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Would you -- I beg your pardon. Yes, okay. Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: To go back to the period after May 1991, and yesterday you were describing the events that took place then, and the situation as it was in Vukovar after that. I'm interested in the following: Did you know that in Vukovar at the time there was a change of directors in certain companies. Those of Serb origin were removed and replaced by those of Croatian origin. Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge I can't answer that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We're still talking about May, June and July of 1991. Did you hear explosions during the night in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They occurred more in Borovo Naselje than where we were. In Vukovar it was -- it appeared as late as July, but in Borovo Selo, it started prior to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you also hear bursts from automatic rifles fired from moving vehicles during that period?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time everyone was nervous and upset, and any sort of movement became suspicious, to be honest.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where did Martin Dosen's brothers live at that time, Tadija and Ivan? What part of Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tadija lived in his apartment block at Dunavska 1, and Ivan, aka Braco, lived with their mother at Olajnica number 12, the same as myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: We know more or less where Olajnica is. What about Dunavska, what part of Vukovar that is, that's where Tadija used to live?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are two high-rises, both on the banks of the Danube. That is close to Castle Eltz.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said that your husband was a professional fisherman. In June, July and early August of 1991, did he ever come across a corpse in the Danube while fishing?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. For your information, he helped a lot of Serbs to cross the Danube. He used his boat.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, why were the Serbs running across the Danube? Why were they crossing the Danube?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I am not aware of them being in any danger, at least as far as I'm concerned, as well as my family. As for their other reasons, they are the only one who could answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said that you didn't know of any danger to them, but did any of your Serb friends tell you that they feel threatened?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They never said they were scared, but they simply said that they didn't like what was happening and that they'd prefer to leave, and so they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you told us that at a certain point Vukovar residents organised themselves and organised guard duties so that one couldn't reach the centre of the town from the nearby villages. Therefore, that was the effective control of entry into the city. I'm interested in the existence of barricades in the outskirts of Vukovar, such as Borovo Selo, Sajmiste and Mitnica?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I am going to speak about Sajmiste and Mitnica, I can only tell you what I heard and what other people were talking about, but personally I never left the centre of the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did Martin Dosen's brothers at a certain point join the National Corps Guard?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe Tadija was performing guarding duty; and Ivan, I believe he was with Mercep. They used to see them together. Yet again I need to reiterate that I spent most of my time with the children, and I don't know what the men were doing and what decisions they made.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether Martin Dosen's son Alen also joined National Guards Corps, and do you know that he was wounded at a certain point?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that. Alen used to come from Borovo Naselje to Vukovar and he was wounded then. I don't know whether he was with the National Guards Corps or whether he just performed guarding duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about Martin Jakubovski? Did he belong to any military formation in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Little Martin did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I believe he did belong to the National Guards Corps.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was a registered member.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you told us where your husband was during the combat operations in Vukovar. I'm interested in whether he was a reserve officer within the military formation that he served with?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't a reserve officer. He was a candidate for an officer and he received that from the Ministry of Defence, but this has been awarded to him posthumously. During the operations in Vukovar, he held no rank.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, he was posthumously awarded the rank of warrant officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you mentioned some other events in Vukovar of 1991, and you said that Martin was wounded for the first time in August 1991. Can you tell me what was the second time that he got wounded, when was that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was wounded the second time when Tadija's nephew Velibor was killed. His body was in the street, and Martin learned of that and he tried to pull him out, to remove the body, and his mother at that time still didn't know that he was killed. From the direction of the Danube, he was hit by a -- by a sniper and he had an entrance/exit wound on his upper arm.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you tell the OTP investigators that your husband was wounded for the first time in August, when he was wounded by shrapnel, and the second time in October when he was hit by sniper in his arm. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If you recall, can you tell us who let you know that he was wounded for the second time when he was wounded by a sniper, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Martin came back from the hospital, they treated him there, and they immobilised his arm. After that he came to Olajnica, and he spent all of his time there until he jumped off the balcony and left for the hospital for good.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did he tell you then which doctor saw him at the time and treated him?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Don't hold me to it, I'm not sure whether it was Dr. Aleksijevic or Dr. Njavro. It was one of the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: If you remember, could you tell me the following: On that occasion was it a wound caused by bullet that went through the muscles, or did it -- did the bullet break any bones? Were there any complications?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The bullet went through the muscle tissue, not through the bone.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately you no longer possess the original hospital documents concerning this particular wounding, I suppose? When he was wounded for the second time by the sniper. Do you have any medical records?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not for that wounding.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: As you told my learned friend from the Prosecution yesterday, for certain administrative purposes you obtained an opinion from Dr. Aleksijevic about your husband's injuries. And that document was admitted into evidence under number 174. Can you tell us on the basis of what Dr. Aleksijevic wrote the findings entitled "case history" or the history of the illness?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because Dr. Aleksijevic treated him at the Vukovar Hospital. And I needed the document in order to be able to prove this for Martin. Since he was absent, I had to prove that it was him, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, madam, I've gathered that much. So Mr. Aleksijevic had no documents, no hospital files on the basis of which to draw up the report. He did it from memory, right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is also indicated in the second document, and I've got the original, and it says why Martin was hospitalised as of the 16th of December [as interpreted] 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, in the report drafted by Mr. Aleksijevic it does not say that the patient was shot through a muscle. It refers to a right elbow that he was shot at, plus a complicated damaged bone. And it is totally different from what you've told us from what you know, basically.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not a medical doctor. Presumably Dr. Aleksijevic is more of an expert than I am. All I knew was that he was shot. As to what complications there were, perhaps there were complications when Martin fell, because the arm had already been immobilised, and then maybe when he fell the bones of the elbow had been further damaged. But when he fell off the balcony the arm had already been injured before, so maybe he sustained further injuries after the fall.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I was just waiting for the translation to come through. You said that the muscle was damaged. Do you feel that there might be a possibility that the wound was actually more along the lines of the description provided by Dr. Aleksijevic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have every trust and confidence in Dr. Aleksijevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. You told us yesterday about how on the 16th of November your husband sustained the injury because of which he was taken to the Vukovar Hospital on that day. Can you tell me, you mentioned to my colleague that you moved from your house to the apartment in Olajnica. As of then, did you spend all of your time in that apartment on the third floor of that building with your husband and daughter?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: How many floors were there in that building, can you tell me?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Seven.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So it's one of the rare high-rises in Vukovar. There were not that many, right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an entire neighbourhood, which is called Olajnica, and there are 18 buildings there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And in other parts of Vukovar, apart from Borovo Naselje, am I correct in saying that most of the buildings were low and that there were no other high-rises there, except in the neighbourhood called Olajnica?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you're wrong there, because there were three or four different neighbourhoods with tall buildings in Vukovar. Around the hospital, behind the hospital, and in the direction of Sajmiste. I won't go into the whole list, but there are at least three or four different neighbourhoods.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, had you heard about people staying in their apartments in all of those neighbourhoods or did they spend their time in shelters?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those buildings, at least in the case of Olajnica, I mean not a single one of those buildings had a cellar or a shelter of any sort. There was just one shelter, purpose-built shelter before the war, in case of need. But there were quite a few people there, so not everyone from that neighbourhood could fit in, so people stayed in their apartments.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I suppose you are talking about the nuclear shelter, which was built for special purposes?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Were you not afraid to stay in a multi-storey building in spite of what you told us yesterday about the intensity of the attacks on Vukovar, did you not fear for your life or the life of your daughter?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. I was scared. And that's why I haven't come to the courtroom, because I suffer from claustrophobia, and I can't be in close spaces, and we just couldn't get out of the buildings. And now I still suffer the consequences. And we couldn't fit into any shelters because there was just not enough room for everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could you not look for another shelter, since your husband worked in the immediate vicinity of the Crisis Staff in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we couldn't go there, because there were no women and children there, and my husband didn't want us to be there. He wanted us to stay with other women and children. He wanted for us to be surrounded by other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you told us that you were observing artillery attacks on people who went to collect water. Can you tell us where from could you observe that and what part of the year was it, what season? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember. It was as late as October; it was getting cold. We didn't have any windows, and my flat faces the house where the well was, because the whole building faces the row of those houses there, and so I could see the well quite clearly from my apartment. I could see the house, and the well was in the courtyard of that house.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: So the well was amongst several houses, if I have understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's in a courtyard of a specific house.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And then next to it there is another house and then another house on the other side? That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. It's just that there were no houses left because they had all been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you agree with me that a well in such surroundings would not have been easily and readily visible?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps so, but perhaps there were other wells. Later on it turned out that the -- there was the chartered surveyor who was in charge of all those arctic wells and he was at the barracks. I can't actually remember the name of the man and I don't know him myself, but I heard stories from other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did he belong to the group of people that you called reserve -- reservists yesterday, mostly locals?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may be true, but I can't really claim it with any degree of certainty because I don't know the man, but I heard other people talking about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And was it somebody from Vukovar or somebody who had come from somewhere else? What did you hear? Was it somebody local?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I heard he was local.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me whether you have ever heard about the existence of -- about the Territorial Defence, the Serb Territorial Defence Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us how far that well was from your high-rise building?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps a hundred metres. I don't want to overdo it. Roughly speaking, a hundred metres, as if the other end of a large-ish courtyard.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Isn't it rather close? If you could see shells landing that close, weren't you afraid that you might be hit in your apartment?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, if you have no water, and you ask somebody to bring some water to you, you accept to watch at least. We had had to learn how to live with fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I can understand that you've reconciled yourselves to a life in fear, but did you also accept the fact that something might happen to your daughter?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. My daughter, in much the same way as I did, knew that we had nowhere else to go, that we had to be there, and we learned how to live under such circumstances. And I can tell you that there were Serb children and -- women and children of Serb nationality on the same floor of the building, and during the war we got along fine, and my then neighbours are still living there, and we still lived together peacefully and well, and I can claim this 100 per cent. We learned how to live together in that corridor, basically.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When did your building take first hit; can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our building, well, the roof of our building and the seventh and the sixth floor were blown off, basically, as early as mid-October. There was no roof left, and the sixth and the seventh floors where missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There were any other hits, or was it the only time that your building was hit in October?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At some point in September, or the beginning of October, my mother-in-law's flat was hit as well and the entire balcony fell off. So my mother-in-law and my sister-in-law's children came down to where we were on the third floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You mentioned the 16th of November and how you were inside the building and the building was hit. You came out of the building and your husband stayed behind to help your neighbour.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you actually know what went on in the building? Did you ask him or was it just an assumption? I mean what you said yesterday, did you just assume that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tanja and myself ran out of the building because Martin told us to get out, and we got out together with other neighbours. And one flat was hit, and there was heating oil there and it caught fire, and so there was a lot of smoke, and my husband could no longer see anything. He couldn't even see the stairs, so he stayed on that floor. But we were standing in front of the building and we were shouting to him to try and come down, but he didn't dare. He didn't dare go through all that smoke. And then we tried to get a rope to him so that he could come down from the balcony, but considering his weight and his injured hand, he just couldn't take it anymore, and between the two floors he fell off, basically, and Tanja and myself were in front of the building. We watched.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, you mentioned that yesterday. What I'm interested in now is you said that he stayed behind in order to help out an elderly neighbour who lived in the same building and you said that this elderly lady actually came down the stairs and got out of the building. Now, why didn't Mr. Martin get out of the building as well together with her? Did you ask him about it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did ask him afterwards at the hospital. But he told me that she told him that there was somebody in the neighbouring flat as well, that she heard some movement, and so he went to see. And then the lady in question had come out, and she said Martin is still in the building. I think there's somebody else. But then it turned out it was just a parrot, and so basically Martin stayed behind because of that parrot, and he no longer could exit the building through the stairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said that you got a rope to him. How did you manage to do that since he was on the third floor of the building? Who managed to do that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were other men in the building who did not go to any fighting positions, and there were two -- I don't know, they were not from our building, so I don't know exactly who they were, but they tied a rope and they got a kind of pole and they were swinging the rope from the pole up until the moment they actually managed to catch the railing of the balcony, and so that's how they got the rope to Martin.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And since you said they were men, didn't they try to get into the building and help him out by the staircase? Did you not ask them to do something like that before he tried coming down a rope from the balcony as you described?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Tanja was almost hysterical. She was crying and she was crying for her father, and so I was very busy trying to calm her down, because she could see that Martin set out from that balcony and she was fully aware that he would not make it, and so she was crying really hard. And at that particular moment, well, I -- I didn't have time to think. I didn't have time to think why nobody else went back into the building and tried to help him that way. I would have been happy if somebody had gone in to help him, but I myself was not brave or strong enough to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You told us that Mr. Martin was transported to hospital and that you and your daughter stayed behind in the building. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you repeat the question, please? Because I haven't heard you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: No problem, just a moment. I asked you: After this event, Mr. Martin was taken to hospital, and you and your daughter Tanja stayed behind in that building, right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Martin was taken to hospital, but Tanja and myself did not stay in the building anymore, because our flat was burnt down, so we moved to the building number 14.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Who were you with in that building?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were looking for empty flats, and whenever we saw that there was an empty flat, we would just go in. Nobody asked any questions about whose flat it was. If it was empty -- people were just looking for a roof over their heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, do you remember how Mr. Martin was dressed on that day, on the 16th of November? If you remember, that is.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly what trousers he had on. I think -- well, I think he had a kind of jeans, and a V-necked vest, because he couldn't wear a jumper because his arm was in a cast, and -- and a checked shirt was thrown over him when he was on the stretcher. That's what I did. And then when I came to the hospital, I could see that his trousers were gone. He only had his swimmers on, basically, and this V-necked vest.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You are telling us that he had this sleeveless vest and a pair of trousers, but this is the month of November, your windows had been shattered. Why wasn't he wearing warmer clothes?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a dining-room in our flat, and Martin had put nylon sheeting over windows and he managed to get an oil stove and we could heat the room and so it wasn't all that cold there. Obviously when he left to go out he would throw a jacket over his shoulders. But when he fell off the balcony, he didn't really have time to think about getting dressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know, since you didn't accompany him, but did you find out later whether upon arrival at hospital he was registered, entered into the hospital books and who was the doctor who admitted him and treated him first, and do you know what the diagnosis was?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I came to visit him at the hospital, when I talked to him, he just told me that he was examined by Dr. Aleksijevic and that he told him that according to his knowledge, since they didn't have an X-ray machine, but he was an orthopaedic surgeon as well, Dr. Aleksijevic, and he told him that according to his experience, he thought that the second, the third and the fourth vertebrae were broken, and he didn't know whether any nerves had been damaged. And he said that he should be treated somewhere else. When they could be evacuated, he said that he should be examined more thoroughly. That's what Martin told me. As to who was the doctor who actually admitted him, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did he mention anything about being examined by Dr. Juraj Njavro on that occasion or not?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Martin didn't tell me that Dr. Juraj Njavro examined him as well, but they were on the same team. As to who was allocated to whom, I really can't help you much with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us what Mr. Martin was wearing when you went to visit him at the hospital? What did he look like? What was he wearing?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had this V-necked brown vest and a pair of swimmers. He didn't even have pyjamas.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did he have his cast?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was he wearing anything else?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: He had no other plaster, apart from the splint on his arm?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you came there, was he lying on a bed or on a stretcher?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: On a bed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did he have a pillow, a blanket on that bed, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did. He had both.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When you came, was he on his back, on his side, or on his stomach?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was on his back. When I came he told me he was starving. I had some bread with me, and I spread some pate over a slice of bread, but I had to lift his bed up, at least the part where his head was, because he couldn't move from his waist up. Otherwise his head would tilt backwards. Therefore, I raised that part of his bed and gave him some food.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could he move his limbs?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He could move his arms. When I was lying next to his feet, he didn't react, didn't move. Later on he said that he felt some warmth when I was lying there. I don't know whether through additional treatment he would get his legs back or not, but the fact is that he couldn't get off the bed and stand on his own two feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Could he move his legs at all? Were you able to observe that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I asked him to move his legs, he replied he couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember saying to the OTP investigator as part of the statement we had mentioned, did you tell him that you told him that Martin injured his spine, that he couldn't walk, but could move his legs, although he couldn't stand? Do you remember saying that to that particular investigator?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There may have been some misunderstanding there because I said he could move his arms and not his legs. He did move his arms. He used them, but not his legs. I apologise, I'm quite certain I said that he could move his arms but not his legs, because he was unable to stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: It is possible, but I was just reading from the statement, has this statement been read out to you in Croatian, and did you sign it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe you when you say that you read from the statement, but I really don't remember that I read the same thing, otherwise I would have warned them. Therefore, I offer my apologies if this is my fault.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mrs. Tuma.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt here. I would like to suggest if the witness are advised to read from the statement or confirm what is said in the statement, then that the witness should have that statement in front of her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We haven't quite reached that point yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm sure Mr. Vasic will keep it in mind if he reaches that point.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour. I tried to save some time and to try to deal with this in a less painful manner, and I believe it has been dealt with, to a certain extent. Otherwise, there is no -- it's not necessary to put the witness -- put the statement before the witness due to the technical difficulty of the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, madam. Can you confirm, based on what Dr. Aleksijevic put together the report you used to prove the status of your husband and to establish the rights that you had, the first time you mentioned it, you said that he wrote that from his memory because he had no documentation, the first event of wounding. What about the event of the 16th of November? Do you know what it is that he used to back up the report and the case history?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I brought the documentation I had to Dr. Aleksijevic, those are the records from the hospital, and based on the findings stipulated on the back of the paper. And he told me that on that first occasion he admitted Martin to the hospital and that he was familiar with his injuries. That's how he wrote the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You will agree, I believe, that there is an inconsistency between what you told us today about where Martin Dosen was injured on the 16th of November and what is stated in the report included in the case history? Dr. Aleksijevic wrote there that Mr. Dosen was injured on the front line and not at home?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you able to remember what you told the OTP, Mrs. Dosen? If not, you could have a look at the statement. But if you can remember, well, then, if you can, answer Mr. Vasic's question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I remember that statement. Perhaps I could take a look. In any case, Dr. Aleksijevic wrote the statement in Zagreb after the exile in order to prove Martin's status. Since he was still considered a missing person, I had to prove that he was in the hospital in Vukovar and that he went missing from there. I had to prove that it was him, and then I used the documentation I had from the Vukovar Hospital. And having in mind that Dr. Aleksijevic treated Martin in the hospital, he defined his general status, including the injuries sustained after the fall. He said that Martin was in his -- on his position because he was keeping guard inside the building. That's why Dr. Aleksijevic thought that that was where Martin was deployed, that that was his position there inside the building. That's why he formulated it in such manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, madam.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said that on the 17th, in the evening, you went to the hospital. Would you agree with me if I told you that we heard from several witnesses that the shelling of Vukovar lasted until the 17th of November and that it ceased afterwards, although there was still some shooting from small arms? Would you agree with such a statement? That is that there was no shelling after the 17th?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: With all due respect, but I wouldn't agree. You should believe us that that night of the 17th, when we moved from Adica, if you know where that forest is, you could hear shelling and there was shelling, indeed. I wouldn't tell you something that never happened. Take my word for it, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What about the very centre of Vukovar and the hospital itself? Was there any shooting and shelling there, or were there -- was there shelling just next to Adica?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time when we reached the hospital we no longer heard any shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, madam. Yesterday you mentioned that the people of Vukovar learned that they should go to the hospital because of the evacuation as early as the 17th. Can you tell us who told them that, and who provided such information to them, if you know?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I mentioned, Martin, who was in the hospital, knew that there was going to be an evacuation and he sent two guys who were in the hospital who could walk to come to our building. When I was leaving the building I didn't want to leave by myself, so I told some of the neighbours, they told some other people. And everyone had some their own family wounded in the hospital, and they all tried their best to tell everyone else to go to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: After your arrival to the hospital, did you hear that Dr. Bosanac told her medical staff to tell the civilians to go to Velepromet and not to the hospital and that Mrs. Zeljka Zgonjanin from the Red Cross in Vukovar was supposed to organise the transport from the hospital to Velepromet so that the civilians would then be evacuated from Velepromet?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. I was present when we were told to go to Velepromet. Personally, I wanted to be in the hospital because of my husband, but half of the people left from the hospital to Velepromet to be evacuated from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, madam. Yesterday you explained to us why you decided to remain in the hospital. You also said that on the 18th you saw Mr. Marin Vidic and Ms. Vesna Bosanac in the hospital. Could you confirm that indeed, did you see Mr. Marin Vidic at the time in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw Mrs. Vesna Bosanac, and Mr. Vidic, I didn't see him. I saw the two of them leave, but as far as their coming back is concerned, I only saw Dr. Bosanac.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yesterday during examination-in-chief you said that you heard later that Mrs. Bosanac went to negotiate the evacuation on the 18th. If I were to tell you that Dr. Bosanac herself said that she went to negotiate evacuation to Negoslavci on the 19th, would you allow for the possibility that you may be confused about the dates?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there is such a possibility. A lot of time passed. I'm no longer certain about the dates or the hour of the day. More or less all of the days were the same, and it is difficult to remember particular days. I am quite certain, though, that it was in the evening, and that she did return. Whether it was precisely on the 18th or the 19th, I am not certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you, madam. Just another detail regarding Dr. Bosanac. You said that she was brought back in the evening and that she was kept inside a room that was guarded. Mrs. Bosanac did not say that she was brought during the evening and that she was kept in a room in the hospital. Are you quite certain as to what you mentioned before? Did you see that or not?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I came out, when -- behind the door where the wounded were, there is an office, and Dr. Bosanac went into the office and in front of the door there were two regular JNA soldiers. Whether she was kept there or whether they were there for her safety, I don't know. But that's what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have another question concerning the 20th. When you mentioned that women and children were told to go to the buses at Ivo Lola Ribar Street, apart from the women and children, were there any men in the group? Can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: How should I put it? It wasn't forming a group but, rather, we were told that civilians, women and children go to the left, and the wounded to the right to the buses. To speak frankly, there were very few men in the convoy. Particularly on the bus where I was with my family, there were only two men there. I believe one of them was a Red Cross driver and he had his ID. He was one of the medical staff. So he was on board, the only male, plus the driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday you mentioned the story concerning the necklace made up of children's fingers. If you can remember, how did you come to learn of that story? Where did you hear of that, that the pregnant woman, Mrs. Markobasic, allegedly possessed such a photograph and that she took that photograph with the necklace? When did you hear of that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that when she was put against a fence, and they were telling her, "You Ustasha whore, where is the necklace made of children's fingers." That's what I heard in front of the hospital. And not before.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What about later? Did you hear anything later about that and whether there was any link between her husband and the story itself, that is the children's fingers, when did you hear about that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did hear that people were saying that her husband was this and that sort of person. And people discussed this also in the hotel where we were in exile. People were simply passing on rumours. I did hear such stories, but personally I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mrs. Dosen, thank you for your answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this concludes my cross-examination. I have no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vasic. Would you like the 20 minutes now, Mr. Borovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it's truly 20 minutes, then yes. But I believe there is even less, hence, I would like to have a break, although I will have just a few questions. If I still have 20 minutes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You misunderstood me. I meant the 20 minute break now. Would you like to have that?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mrs. Dosen, we will have a break now for 20 minutes and then Mr. Borovic will have some questions for you. We will resume at five minutes to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Borovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mrs. Dosen. I am the defence counsel for Miroslav Radic.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You said today that the Serbs didn't like what was going on and therefore they started leaving, and when you were asked why exactly in more detail, you said you didn't know. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the statement you gave to the OTP, and of course you did not argue with the authenticity of that statement, you said that tension started to mount after the -- after Croatia was declared independent. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't a declaration of independence as yet, but it was between the police and the MUP and the Croatian coat of arms and some officers refused to wear it on their uniforms. And that's, in my view, where these tensions first started. That's what I heard from my talks and rumours and conversations I had with my neighbours, because I tended to see more women rather than men. But there were stories going around about how these people simply could not accept replacing the red star by the Croatian coat of arms. That's at least what I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now on the second page of your statement that you made in Croatian, it says that tension started to mount in Vukovar after Croatia declared independence, and then afterwards you said that Serb police officers refused to wear the coat of arms and to accept it and embrace it as their flag. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know from your history lessons that in 1941 the Independent State of Croatia, which was led by the Ustasha was set up?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did hear about it at school.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you know that their flag also bore the Croatian coat of arms?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that from school.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you think that might have been the reason why Serb police officers might have refused to wear the Croatian coat of arms? Could that have been one of the reasons, their memories of that Independent State of Croatia of old? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Perhaps, yes, they didn't accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you familiar with the fact that after World War II, actually many years later, there was a trial of Andrija Artukovic in Zagreb? And, first of all, do you know who know Andrija Artukovic was?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I know is what I saw on TV. And I was taught at school that he was one of the Ustasha leaders. As far as I can recollect. But I myself was never in favour of either the Ustasha or the Chetniks, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't casting doubt on that. But when you said that you learned at school about him being a leader of the Ustashas, does it mean that he was one of the leaders of that independent fascist Ustasha state of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Presumably.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was he put on trial for war crimes in Zagreb and the victims were Serbs? What I have in mind is Jasenovac in the first place. Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw it on TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said in your statement to the OTP, and you commented on that both yesterday and today, about you having heard that the HDZ purchased 700 Kalashnikovs and guns. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When did you hear about that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At some point in August. I think it was in August.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you said that your husband bought a Kalashnikov and a gun in order to keep his family safe. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have joint -- joint finances with your husband? Did you know what the other spouse was spending money on?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, I'm one of those people who are not good with money, and for the most part it was my husband's domain. All I cared about was to have everything I needed around the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But do you know how much he paid for that Kalashnikov and his gun, the ones that you had for your own household needs?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the best will in the world, I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know whether he provided any financial support for the purchase of those 700 Kalashnikovs? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Have you ever heard anything about that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did hear about Martin being a donor for the HDZ party. But as to whether it had anything to do with the purchases of arms or just with party activities, I wouldn't know. But he was a donor for the party, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did HDZ, as a political party, have a military wing in the course of the war, and did that military wing carry the name ZNG?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the ZNG existed in Vukovar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Where did your husband keep his Kalashnikov in the course of the war? Did you see that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he came back from his guard duty, he only had the gun, and I suppose the Kalashnikov was kept where he was on duty. But when he was on -- when he was wounded --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And where was he on duty, where was he on guard duty, that's my question?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At Nama.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was that where he was deployed for his military duty?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you said today that he bought the Kalashnikov and the gun for keeping his family safe, so what happened to the family? I mean, we mentioned the weapons that he had on his guard duty, but what about the family weapons?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he was shot he came to Olajnica, and that's when he brought the Kalashnikov home as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And when he was taken to hospital, did he take the Kalashnikov with him or did he leave it to you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Kalashnikov and the gun stayed in the flat and went up in flames with the rest of the stuff in the flat, and Tanja and myself didn't take it out.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And could the counsel please wait for the witness to finish the statement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You said that your husband was on guard duty. Was he on guard duty or not?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: At what period in time? Did you hear my question?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: At what period -- at what point in time was he on guard duty in your building?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: From when he was first shot, by the end of October. When he was shot in the arms and when he was hospitalised then came home and he had this splint and then he came to Olajnica, and that's where he was on guard duty, as protection for the women and children who were in the building because there were only a couple of men there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And were other people in the same building on guard duty or was he on his own 24 hours a day?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Other people were on guard duty as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did they carry weapons as well?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did, but I didn't see any of that. Presumably they had weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you have the names of any of the people in your building who were on guard duty in the same way?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No names. I know about two people who were with Martin. To tell you the truth, I don't really remember what their names was. Martin used to call them George and Bush, but we were there only for three months, so I really don't know. I didn't know these people by their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know how old they were?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were about 50 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us now at what point in time your husband used to work at the Crisis Staff? This is something that you already mentioned in your statement to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he wouldn't come home at night. It was probably as early as August, up until the time when he was shot. During the day he would come home to see Tanja and myself, up until the point when the shell landed on our house, and then we went to Olajnica. We went to Olajnica, and he would visit us during the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know anything about your husband's membership in the Crisis Staff? What was his position there and was he a prominent member?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean? Crisis Staff or where he was on guard duty?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Was he a member of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And could the counsel please not interrupt the witness because we can't listen to both at the same time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was he a member of the Crisis Staff, I don't know. But he did used to go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: And did you know whether Dr. Vesna Bosanac was a member of the Crisis Staff in Vukovar -- or, rather, did your husband ever tell you that he used to meet her there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Martin never told me about having been in touch with Vesna Bosanac or that she was at the Crisis Staff when he used to go there. I really can't confirm that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned that high-rise buildings such as yours also existed in the vicinity and behind the hospital. That's what you said in answer to my colleague's, Mr. Vasic's question; is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How far are those high-rise buildings from the hospital, the ones that are closest to the hospital, in fact, in your view?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my opinion, the ones that are behind the hospital might be at a distance of about 100 or even 50 metres. You simply cross the street and that's where the first building is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what about the ones next to the main entrance to the hospital? How far are they?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ones in front of the hospital are slightly further away because they're next to the bridge, across the Danube. It's an entire neighbourhood, which is on the bank of the river. So perhaps 300 metres away, according to my estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now to back to the ones behind the hospital. Are you aware of the fact that shots were fired from there aimed at the JNA or not?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know. It was at the hospital, and I was further away.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you were asked whether you knew about the ZNG formations in Vukovar, you said yes. But did you ever hear about the HOS military formations or the Croatian defence powers or whatever?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Were there any such formations in Vukovar itself, I don't know, but I met a couple of young boys at the hospital who said that they belonged to the HOS, and now I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you know that there were the so-called Domobrans as well during the war?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I haven't heard of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you hear about what military formations were called Ustasha? Did you hear anything about that? Was it the ZNGs?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I myself did not see anyone bearing the Ustasha insignia, and that's why it is really not clear to me why they should be declared as Ustasha extremists, amongst them my husband as well, and they were not really.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Fine, if you don't know. We talked of Martin Jakubovski and you said that he was a registered member of the ZNG. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me himself that he had been to Opatovac and that he signed some papers there and that he registered. And he came back from the army and that's what he said to me himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you see Martin Jakubovski on the 17th of November when you came to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What was he wearing when you found him at the hospital? Was he wearing a military uniform, since he was a member of the ZNG or what?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had had surgery because he was hit in the arm and he almost lost his hand, and Dr. Aleksijevic managed to save it. And he had a pair of pyjamas and the hospital gown.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And when he was brought in, as you mentioned to the OTP, perhaps I should read it out from your statement. It's page 5, last paragraph. And you said that Martin Jakubovski was brought in. What was he wearing at that particular moment?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he was brought to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: No, on the bus.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he was brought to the bus, I think he was wearing the same clothes, but he also had a jacket and he had some kind of pink pullover.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you say to the OTP that he was a well-known marksman, and did you say that his position was on the roof of the high school? That's my first question. Did you say that to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, he told me that he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you also say to them that from that position on the roof of the high school he was shooting at the JNA planes from that roof? Can you confirm that you said that to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's -- it was from the roof of the grammar school, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is the grammar school a high school?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But the grammar school was situated a bit out of town, further away from the centre of town. That's what I meant to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And what Martin Jakubovski tell you about the activities from the roof of the grammar school and about the shooting of the JNA planes? When was it, did he manage to shoot any planes down, or do you remember anything about that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I asked him about where he was in the course of all those events and all those times, the shooting and bombing, et cetera, because his parents were not there, they were at Vinkovci, and he was staying with his grandmother in Vukovar, and so I was a bit worried about him. And then he said, "Aunt, I am at the grammar school, I am on the roof, and we are trying to defend ourselves from the planes." Those were his words. As to whether he shot anything, how he shot anything down, I have no idea, because I wasn't there. Whether any of the planes came down, I can't tell you because he never said anything about that. I simply asked him where he was, just so I knew whether he was alive or not. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But you confirmed that a part of your statement was the fact that he was a famous marksman. What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, his had nickname was Spegelj, and his friends used to tell me that he was a rather good marksman. But to what extent he was good or bad, I have no idea because I was never there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Obviously you are not a witness who should provide us detailed information about these circumstances, but since you did mention that he was operating a canon shooting the planes, do you know what kind of canon it was since your husband and his brother seemed to have been in the army. Have you ever talked about it? Was it an anti-aircraft gun or some other kind of gun or canon or do you not know?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea, believe me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I do believe you. You mentioned the month of May 1991 and the fact that police officers were killed in Borovo Naselje. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Borovo Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that on that occasion quite a few Serbs were injured and that with heavy injuries they were taken to the Vukovar Hospital. Those were injuries caused by fragmentation bullets, right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only tell you what I heard and about the information we saw on TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Just this one question in relation to Serbs: Have you ever heard that, did you hear that --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe I have a problem with the recording. I don't know if this is all right in the transcript. In order to avoid any problems later, I would like to make sure that everything is getting into the transcript. At least I don't seem to be able to hear well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There had been no indication that what is being said is not being heard and will therefore appear in the transcript. There is, however, an ongoing problem. I suspect that you are listening to the B/C/S, and when the speaker stops you then move to your question, whereas the translation in other languages is continuing, and in particular in English, and so that you are often putting the next question while the translation of the last answer is continuing. And I think that is causing difficulties for those who are trying to hear and translate what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You put it very elegantly, but I'm basically the problem, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: My next question now. Today we heard about the war duties of your husband today and about how he was placed at the Nama department store.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did you report him missing with the ministry for missing persons, and did you provide any data to the ministry?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Were you the only witness providing data about missing persons?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were more people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I mean in conjunction with your husband. Were you the only one or were there more witnesses?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was providing data for my husband, but his sister did the same, because she didn't know what happened to him, so she reported him missing as well. Whoever had a member of the family missing, they all tried to provide as much data as possible in order to be able to find something out. So it is indeed possible that other people had gone and provided data and reported him missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In what year was your husband awarded his military grade as warrant officer by the defence ministry?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have that document at home and I really can't remember. If you have the document in front of you, it might be easier, because I don't want to make a mistake. I do have the paper at home, but I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was it before you reported him missing or afterwards?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Did he get that before you reported him missing or afterwards?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Later.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was he a member of the so-called Vukovar Brigade?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As to whether he was a member of that brigade or not, on the papers he got from his commander it says that he was carrying out guard duties at the Nama department store. That's what it says on the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you were describing his fall from the balcony, you said he was taken to the hospital on a stretcher and you also said that there used to be stretchers in buildings at the time. That's what you said yesterday, right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As of when were those stretchers there, who brought them to the buildings and why were they there? First of all, I would like to know as of what point in time were there stretchers in your building.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When exactly they were brought in, I do not know. But when I came to the building the stretchers were already there, because the nuclear shelter that existed at Olajnica could not take all the inhabitants of Olajnica and so they needed more space. But what they did then, they left a couple of stretchers in every building, in case of need, in case somebody was wounded or if there was shelling, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were they brought by the ZNG soldiers, that is the National Guards Corps?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was some degree of organisation inside the shelter itself, but I can't tell you who managed that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you saw Martin Jakubovski, aka Spegelj, in the hospital, my question is the following: Did Binazija Kolesar do the same thing to him as she did with your husband? Did she provide him with the medical report so that he could use it after the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, she did that with each of the wounded and the wounded were supposed to have it with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: I asked you specifically about Martin Jakubovski.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, because Martin was in the corridor. You had to go through the room to reach him, and I didn't see whether he was holding the documents in his hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about Ivan and Tadija Dosen? Were they also given the medical records?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ivan was not wounded; he had no documentation. He came with us from Olajnica, and he wasn't in the hospital as one of the wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: What about Tadija?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was wounded, I couldn't see him clearly, because he was already on the bus. He was in the hospital overcoat, but I couldn't see whether he had anything in his arms. He could walk by himself, and he left the room before Martin did.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us the name of a person, any other person who had their medical record in their hands, apart from yourself?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about the civilians. I took the plastic bag given to me, but each of the wounded had the same on them, and they probably took the papers with them. As to why those documents are now missing, I don't know, but each of the wounded was given their set.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: It seems only logical to ask you the following: Irrespective of the fact that your husband was on a stretcher, why wasn't the documentation given to him and why didn't he have that when he was being carried to the bus, rather the papers remained in your hands and all the other wounded had their papers with them?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't explain. I know I picked those papers up from his bed before he was put on a stretcher as he needed to be moved from the bed on to the stretcher, and the papers were on the bed. That's why I picked up this plastic bag.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
