utterances.text: Thank you. You stated that you saw three JNA soldiers in the hospital. My question is: How did you recognise them? How did you know they belonged to the JNA and yet you had spent only one day in the hospital prior to that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The three soldiers in the Vukovar Hospital, they were separated from the rest by a glass, by a window, and Martin told me that they brought in three wounded JNA soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did he tell you when they were brought in?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact date. I believe they had been in the hospital when Martin came in, so they must have been wounded prior to his arrival. Martin said they were fine guys, and they talked, they communicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: You said they were separated by a glass wall. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: How far from your husband?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you for certain. The entire room was filled with beds. Perhaps they were five beds away, if you can picture that in your mind, and then the glass wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Of course, one couldn't hear them talking behind the glass wall?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you then explain for the Chamber what you said yesterday when you said that those soldiers refused to go with the JNA officers who wanted to take them away, to save them, so to speak, or is it true that you did not hear that at all?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that because they said that in the corridor as they were leaving. They left the room that was behind the glass wall, and they had to pass by the other beds. And then they were discussing this with the officer who came to pick them up. They asked him, and I quote, "Why should we now go? We were not in any danger here. We were treated equally, as the rest." That was the conversation I overheard as they passed me by.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Prior to your testimony, that is, your statement with the OTP, were you prepared or coached by any institution in Zagreb to give such a statement?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember any coaching. If you are to believe me, a lot of years passed in the meantime, and there were numerous conversations, people from various centres and institutions came to talk, and I don't want to confuse things.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before you decided, or opted for such testimony, were you coached in any way in Zagreb for this particular testimony? Or to keep it short? Is there such a thing as a centre for the preparation of witnesses to testify in The Hague provided those witnesses are of Croatian nationality?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Preparations, no. I talked about my statement. I don't remember what year you said it was that I gave the statement; I believe 1995. They asked me whether it was correct, that I should reread the statement and just to check whether I still remember what I said in the statement and whether everything was recorded in a proper way. Yes, I did go through that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Who helped you remind yourself of the statement?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe one of the representatives of The Hague Tribunal. I don't know the exact function or the title of the person, but that person was probably from the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Dosen. This concludes my cross-examination. Thank you again.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And thank you, Mr. Borovic. Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic will now have some questions for you, Mrs. Dosen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours, good afternoon to all those present, good afternoon to Mrs. Dosen. My name is Novak Lukic from Belgrade, and I'm counsel for Mr. Sljivancanin. I wanted to ask you some questions. I would like to apologise beforehand to the Chamber and to yourself should some of my questions overlap with the questions put by my colleagues. I did my best to short-list the questions I had after the cross-examination of my colleagues. As it often happens, since we are always to go last, some of the questions are usually put by other colleagues before. That is why I will try to ask you about the things you haven't answered yet. Since I am often warned for not speaking too fast, I will just remind you to make a short pause between my question and your answer so that we would have a clear transcript. I wanted to link up with the topic that Mr. Borovic concluded with. I wanted to ask you whether I have precise information concerning the statements that were at our disposal in which you provided some information about the facts that you are testifying, and you can confirm this perhaps for me. According to the information we have, in 1995 you gave a comprehensive statement to the OTP, and after that there was another short statement in which you were shown sets of photographs in order to recognise some people. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We also received information that you gave a statement to the Ministry of Health of Croatia dated the 14th of April, 1993 whereby you also described the facts you testified about here. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is why I said to your colleague, so as to avoid any misunderstanding, that I gave several statements, but I don't remember precisely to whom and where and when.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You testified before this very Tribunal back in 1998 in Dokmanovic case; that was in February 1998. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Right after you, your daughter came to testify on that day. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What we also know, and you were asked about that by Mr. Borovic, you provided some data as a part of the questionnaire put together by the Republic of Croatia and their centre for the missing persons, and you gave some information concerning the people who went missing from Vukovar, particularly in relation with your missing husband, Mr. Martin Dosen. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We were also told by the OTP, and you confirmed this a while ago, that you spoke with the OTP representatives somewhat recently, I believe not more than a month ago, when you were shown your previous statement. You were reminded of what you said then and then you introduced certain corrections that you deemed necessary?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I believe you will also confirm that when you were given the initial statement back in 1995, and I believe you can be given the statement by the registry representative who is next to you should it become necessary, in addition to the interpreter and the interviewer, your daughter was also present. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When do you think Tanja was present? Could you repeat, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm looking at the statement of the 22nd of August 1995, and as far as we know that was your first interview with Mr. Milner from the OTP and an interpreter, and the statement mentions the presence of your daughter Tanja as well. That's why I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I believe the interview was conducted in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they came to see me, it is likely that Tanja was present as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The way I calculate it, Tanja was 18 and a half back in August 1995, if that is correct.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: She was born on the 10th of January, 1977.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: A fortnight after that an -- OTP representatives interviewed your daughter at the Intercontinental in Zagreb. Were you present during that interview?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Don't hold me to it, but I believe so. We had only one room. At a certain point I was making coffee for everyone, but I believe I was present in the room as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So as not to have any confusion, I read that in the very contents of the statement put together by the investigator. I just wanted to verify. I will move on to another topic, because I believe we now have the framework of the information we had concerning what you know about the events in Vukovar. We hope that the registry representative sitting next to you has all these documents there, and should we need to refer to them, he may assist you in putting them before you, because I will deal in some detail with your previous statements. Before the war and during the conflict back in 1991, did you know Dr. Njavro?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We knew him because his wife was a teacher in school. She taught Tanja.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know Dr. Bosanac before the war, or during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used to know her because -- because she was a paediatrician, that is before she became the head of hospital. As for my husband, I don't know whether he knew her any better. He knew her as a paediatrician as well. Tanja, on the other hand, was good friends with Dr. Bosanac's sons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While we're on the topic, do you know whether any of the sons of Dr. Bosanac was a member of the National Guards Corps or any of the other defensive forces in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really couldn't say. I didn't see them. The first time I saw them was in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know Mr. Marin Vidic, or did your husband tell you that he knew him either before or during the war when he assumed certain positions in Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Martin knew Mr. Vidic from Vukovar. They were acquaintances that would greet each other on the street. Anything more than that, I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I presume you used to know Mr. Vidic from seeing him in the city, you knew what he looked like?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's what we heard from you yesterday. I just wanted to verify whether you knew it was actually him. What about Dr. Aleksijevic? Did you know him during or before the war, apart from the incidents when your husband was injured?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know him before the war. I met him during the war, and we met in Zagreb. I knew his wife better because she used to work in the hospital even before the war. We were not friends, but I knew her as one of the medical staff, a nurse.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In one of your statements to the OTP I read the following; perhaps you can confirm. I believe you said that you were comfortably off before the war, you and your family. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was always a good friend to the people I knew, and for the time we were comfortably off. Martin, myself, and having in mind the number of children we had, we had quite a good life.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I presume most of your income came from the restaurant, or was there any other income within the family in 1990 and 1991?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The income mostly came from fishing, because Martin sold his fish in the marketplace and in some other restaurants. And we used his fish, of course, but our restaurant was only open during summer, when people went to the river-banks, but not during winter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Concerning his HDZ activities that you testified about and his political affiliation and activities, although you did say he was but an ordinary member, was that something that he kept secret, or was he quite public about it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He never -- he was never hiding that. He was public about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Another question in relation to your situation at the time and concerning your reply to my colleague, Mr. Borovic. When he was awarded that military rank posthumously, you said that you received that in a letter from his commander. Do you know who signed the document, who signed it as commander to your husband?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, I believe his name is Krsic. He used to be the managing director of the Nama department store. He was killed, however, trying to break out of Vukovar. And the document, on the other hand, was signed by Mr. Daniel Rehak.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I must be honest, I know nothing of him. Do you know what his title or function was? Did he have anything to do with the association of the Vukovar defenders?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you anything about his title. I do know he was a prisoner and that he was in the camp in Serbia. I used to know him before the war; we were schoolmates. As for his title, I don't know. But as it seems, he was Martin's commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So as not to go again through all the questions concerning your husband's injuries, I wanted to ask you just this, and it still remains unclear. When he was injured for the second time, and you described that, you said that he was injured by a sniper, did he remain in the hospital or was he treated clinically and released immediately?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was treated immediately and released. They said there was no need for him to stay in the hospital and that they are short of space and that there are many people who have more serious injuries, so he was sent home.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As you replied to Mr. Vasic, that was sometime in September?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was at the end of October or maybe even around mid-November.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon for going into such detail, but I believe you were not being specific enough. Perhaps this will help you recall: The second time he was injured by the sniper, how much before his fall from the third floor was it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some 10 days before.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When your husband was brought to the hospital on the 16th, you said you were not present but that you came the next evening. But did you hear either from him or any of the doctors that any sort of treatment was applied in his case, medical treatment?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Martin told me that nothing could be done, because an examination of the spine was needed. What he did tell me is that his arm hurt and that his splint was changed. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Therefore, he was wearing a new splint, and I presume you saw that, compared to the previous one?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The previous one was dirty, and it also broke when he fell off the balcony.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The way I calculate it, you spent some two days next to your husband in the hospital, the 18th and the 19th, provided you came in the evening of the 17th and not counting the 20th when the evacuation took place. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was he prescribed any treatment? Was he receiving medication at the time?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No medication, apart from the painkillers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see his temperature being taken on the 18th? Did you witness that and, if so, at what time of day, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't present when his temperature was taken. When the nurses were supposed to take temperatures and change dressings, I was supposed to leave the room because, in essence, civilians couldn't stay in the room where the wounded were. I was the only one allowed, since he was a broken man and was crying a lot of time; therefore they let me stay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you remember what time of day it was when they were changing dressings? I know we are going into much detail, but we concern ourselves with facts. If you don't know, I won't insist any further.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't want to say something that is incorrect. Some were changed in the morning, some in the evening, depending on the amount of bleeding and the type of help needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there any visible bruises anywhere on his body following the fall and, if so, where? Maybe on his head?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: His face was swollen, but he said that the doctor had told him that it was kind of normal, because of his weight and the fall, and he fell kind of standing up, and so he also had pains in his stomach. And I didn't see the bruises because I didn't look at his body, in fact. I didn't take the blanket off.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. I need to check the transcript. It was a correction, rather. You said that he fell on his feet. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, that's fine. These medical files that ended up in your files, and as you told us yesterday and today, this is the documentation that you had on the 20th in the morning when he was going to be transferred from the bed to the stretcher. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was that the time when the medical files were brought to him next to his sick-bed? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Nurse Biba was placing medical files next to each patient. She was walking through the ward and leaving the medical files by the feet of the bed of every patient. That was meant to serve the purpose of further treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, you've already explained that. When you say Nurse Biba, you mean Binazija Kolesar. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you tell anyone that you were going to keep the medical files and not to leave it next to Martin when he was placed on the stretcher? Did anyone allow you to keep those medical records, any person in particular?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nobody allowed me, but nobody prevented me either. It was just that I thought that since we were following Martin and that I was going to stay with him that I should take it. That's why I took it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Another question in conjunction with these medical files, we saw two documents which referred to that period of time and two previous certificates, first of all the temperature chart, and secondly the form with the handwritten text on the other side. That's the way I see it, so we're talking about two separate papers here. Now, my question is this: Apart from these documents that you have shown to the Court, was there any other document that you did not submit to the Court, and that you still have in your possession? Did you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. We're talking about one document, a single document. It's just that it got torn, so when it was photocopied it ended up as two, but it was like a folded sheet of paper, a single document. We're not talking about two. It's just that it was torn, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So there are no other original documents dated the 20th of November coming from the hospital in your possession. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. With regard to the transcript, page 54, word [as interpreted] 16, my learned friend asked when the medical documents were left on the beds of the patients, and whether it was on the 20th in the morning. I think that the date does not appear in the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said it was on the 20th in the morning. Can we conclude on that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, before the evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you explain a little bit where your husband was? You said next to the door, but I don't know the door to where. Where was his place at the hospital, was it the exit, and if that indeed was the exit from the hospital, which one?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was next to the exit. That was where you could -- it was also the entrance, in fact. There is no other door.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us where the room was? Can you explain that? Because we've explained the structure of the ground floor of the hospital to some extent, so can you tell us where that room was located?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the ground floor. There's nothing else. It's the ground floor, not even an upper floor, just the ground floor. And that's where the surgeries used to be before, where -- a day clinic was there. I used to come and see my gynaecologist there as a young mother, and afterwards it was turned into a single room where the wounded were lying in their beds. But basically those were waiting-rooms before. And that's where I was sitting next to him, and that's where the patients were placed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you enter the area from the main entrance to the hospital?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the main entrance, but behind. Not quite behind, but you have to go around to some extent. It's a bit to the side of the main entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But you said that you visited Tadija Dosen on that first evening, so where was he in relation to where Martin was? Where was his bed?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tadija was -- hmm, can I explain that. It was like a corridor and there was the -- the piping was there, in fact, and extra beds were placed there. It was a corridor of sorts. And that's where he was. It is after the room where Martin was. You go through that room, and then you get to the corridor and other patients were there and that's where Tadija was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what about Martin Jakubovski? Was he anywhere near Martin Dosen? I mean was he in the same room, the same area that you have just described.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Martin was closer to Tadija than to Martin.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about this because when you testified in the Dokmanovic case you said that when you went with Martin and when soldiers started taking him out you said that Martin Jakubovski was already out. Do you remember that? Where did you get that information that those wounded who could walk, who could move, had already been out before your husband was taken out?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not information, that's what happened. They were called, their names were called, and so they came out. And of course the ones who could walk were called first. And then it took time for the nurses to come to place Martin on the stretcher, et cetera. And those injured who could walk, they had already gone out.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did the other people who were at the hospital start leaving at that stage? Did you see that as well, the people whose names had not been called?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were leaving as well, but first they needed to come downstairs from the first floor to that room, because they had to use the same door. But the civilians were on the first floor of the hospital and not where the wounded were. So they had to come down one floor. And of course they were coming out as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, I must check something out. Perhaps it would be best if the secretariat representative could hand you the statement which is on three typed pages. I would like you to read out on page 1, the last paragraph, and you said: "The history of illness of my husband is something I took with me." Can you read the last sentence, please? It starts with: "All those in plaster and wearing white coats." Do you have the statement in front of you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is a document, just so as to help my colleagues from the Prosecution, it's a document which is, according to -- what's revealed to us according to Rule 68, and it is document 2D 090001. But there is no need to place it on the ELMO if the witness is simply going to read out a simple sentence. "All those who were in plaster and wearing white coats." It's the last sentence, the very last sentence on page 1.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, on page 1. "All those in plaster..." I can't see it on page 1. Just a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: May I just ask you, Mrs. Dosen, do you have the document bearing the mark -- it's a typed document, a three-page typed document?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, now I seem to have received it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The last paragraph in the middle. "All of those in plaster..."

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: And those who had put white coats on or had fake plaster-casts. Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you continue, and then the history of the -- two paragraphs lower.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Then I saw some nurses..." Is that the one?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just hang on a moment. Mrs. Dosen, the last paragraph starts with the date, the 19th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "At around 8.00 in the morning, the head nurse Biba..."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you just read it very slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the entire paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, but very slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "On the 19th of November, 1991, in the morning, at around 8.00, head nurse Biba had to draw up a list of all patients and indicate their case histories, as if for evacuation. My husband's case history is something I took with me. All those with plaster and wearing white coats had to be examined by a military doctor and the ambulance drivers had to have their papers, their identity papers."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It doesn't really matter what comes next. What is of importance here is, since there is no signature on this statement but I suppose that you stand by it, is this: Have you heard or seen on that morning that any military doctors had come in there and carried out any examinations? Do you have any recollection of that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen any military doctors, and they didn't enter the room where I was, where the wounded patients were. But they had to go out, the ones who supposedly had fake casts. They were called out and invited to exit through the door. But I myself did not see any military doctors. It was just said that they had to be examined in order to see what degree of injury there was underneath the plaster-casts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hear about any one of them having been examined by a military doctor when you left the premises or when you were standing around with other women?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear anything, because I didn't linger. I left in the direction of the bus, together with the wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know Dr. Ivankovic or Dr. Stanimirovic by any chance? I mean, do you know them by sight, do you know what they look like?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because Dr. Stanimirovic was my GP when I used to work at the factory and he's a psychiatrist now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you come across them in the hospital corridors on that morning?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Ivankovic, yes, but not Dr. Stanimirovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the basis of the statement that you were reading out from earlier, and you could read the next sentence as well. I found it very difficult to read it, truth be told. But you mentioned that head nurse Biba came along with a new list then, and do you remember, do you remember whether Madam Biba was present with those two soldiers when they were reading through, or did she come later when your husband's name was read out?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sister Biba, Nurse Biba was already in the room and she was distributing medical records to other patients when the list was already being read. I'm not saying -- well, I found it weird that they were all on this list, or maybe it was according to the order of admittance to hospital, but they were all on the list, so their names were read out first. So there were -- there was a roll-call of sorts, and the others came out before my husband, because my husband had to be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you get in touch with anyone? Did you ask anyone whether you could accompany your husband and, if so, when?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't talk to anyone that morning, because Martin was really anxious for me to stay with him, and he said, "As soon as I go, you come with me." And since I was allowed to remain close to him, even before the evacuation, I was of the view that it would be only normal and proper for me to continue with this without asking any further permissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Because yesterday on page 43 of the transcript you mentioned that you were allowed to go with Martin. You meant that it was granted by the doctors who knew that he needed to be accompanied by someone because they knew about what state he was in. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Another topic now. And maybe we could have a break then. My understanding was that you and your daughter Tanja walked by Martin's side throughout that time as he was being carried out of the hospital and into the courtyard. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And so you walked past those people who were being searched in front of the entrance to casualty. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me first ask you this: Were you yourself searched?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I myself, no. I went by as the other people were being searched.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that they were looking for sharp objects, weapons, and you even mentioned gold. Did you see that anyone was looking for anything such as gold or valuables or money or anything of the sort? Did you see it yourself?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see any gold or money being taken from anyone, but as I walked past there was a kind of fence, and I could see that people were leaving their nail scissors or nail files stuff like that there. But I can't confirm about the money or gold or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As you were leaving, did you go by the plaster room and did you notice anything amiss there? Do you know where the plaster room was, first of all?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was as you walked from Martin's bed, you had to walk past five or six other beds before you reached the plaster room. And as to whether I noticed anything amiss or anything weird, I can't say so, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have a break now so that I can get my questions organised for the next topic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have a break now, and we will resume at 10 minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Dosen, we may continue and try to wrap things up. Without repeating the entire consequence of events, could you tell me how long did it take for your husband to be put on the stretcher and until the moment he was in front of the bus? Your movement through the corridor and the courtyard as well as the search, that is, how long did that take?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: 10 to 15 minutes, not more.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you described the third bus specifically. Were you able to notice at the moment of your arrival whether the other buses were already full of people?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, mostly. There were some wounded still coming in, but all the other buses were more or less full.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During the period you spent in front of the bus and upon your return to the courtyard, were you able to see whether any people were taken off some of the buses and left standing on the side?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only remember a young man who was taken off a bus by a friend, and he returned him to the hospital. This friend was of Serb nationality, and the young man was a Croat, and he returned him to the hospital and later I saw that young man in Zagreb. It means that his friend managed to save him, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In terms of time, how long were you in front of the bus before you returned to the courtyard, including your conversation with the soldier with Drko and Mr. Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe half an hour or three quarters of an hour, more or less. I don't think it was any longer than that. Although to me it seemed like eternity. It was up to one hour at the most. So anything in between half an hour and a full hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you marked some spots on the photographs in order to corroborate some facts. I wanted to ask you the following: The dialogue you had with the soldier who took the money from Mrs. Markobasic and gave it to you, did it all take place where Martin was on his stretcher or was it somewhere else? And if so, how far away?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was right next to where Martin was. He came off the bus, and then he put the money in my hand. He took Ruzica on the bus and he left her there. This was a young man, a reservist. He was a decent guy. That's why I dared ask him the questions I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tanja was next to you and Martin throughout this time. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your conversation with Drko, was that on the same spot or did you move? Did he come to you, to the place where Martin was?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke with Drko as Martin was being returned to the hospital. I wanted him to return him to the hospital and then perhaps I was hoping that they won't leave him there on the concrete, but that we find some other accommodation for him. So it was at the moment when Martin was still -- was being carried away from the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I may have a moment, please. So you spoke with him after you had spoken with Mr. Sljivancanin. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was when I was going back to -- towards Martin, when the soldiers came to pick him up, and to -- I wanted to go back and take the back. Then Drko came by and I asked him, "Drko, is there anything you can do?" It was again close to the bus, but not at the very spot where Martin's stretcher was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I wanted to quote a part of your testimony in Dokmanovic case, page 55, date the 6th of February, 1998, and I wanted you to comment, please. [In English] "Our locals, the people of Vukovar could not help us, so I told my husband, I'm going to go to the Major and to ask him what I am -- what I and my daughter were doing there." Since you mentioned your conversation with Drko, it follows from what I read that you decided to have this conversation with Mr. Sljivancanin only after that. So which way is it? The way you put it back then, or today?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's something wrong there, because I spoke with Drko only after the conversation I had had with Mr. Sljivancanin. And when I was going back, he appeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Therefore you want to remain with the version you expressed today?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your statement to the OTP, and you have it before you dated 1995, page 6, you also said, that is page 6, the second paragraph from the bottom: "I told Drko ..." Did you find that part?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 6?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The one before last, that's the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is not it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you see the last passage is: "When I realised I would get no help there, I went to see Sljivancanin." Do you see that? Perhaps it is best if I read in B/C/S, and then we can clarify whether there is any doubt as to the translation or the content of your statement. So your statement from 1995, page 6, paragraph -- the second paragraph from the bottom of the page: "I told Drko" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I think the witness may have found the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Dosen, did you locate the paragraph?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I have the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Read in B/C/S and see if she accepts that that is what she said in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to notify the OTP that I am to read from the English version, page 5. [In English] Last two sentences. [Interpretation] "I said to Drko, Help me save my husband. He replied, Be quiet, Dosen. You Dosens have a lot of butter on your heads. This is an expression that means you have a lot to answer for. When I realised that there was to be no help there, I went up to Sljivancanin," and the dialogue follows. Even in that statement given to the OTP you claim that you spoke to Drko first and then went to see Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to interrupt here, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then it must have been like that. I am tired and confused by now.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: So the question, so there will not be any confusion for the witness or any kind of misleading to the witness, concerning yesterday's transcripts, and that is page number 3804, line 8 and 9. There is a question put by me: "Thank you, Mrs. Dosen. You mention here that you had no one else to turn to. Did you make any try before you addressed this tall officer in this respect in order to get some help?" And then the answer follows from the witness: "I tried to speak to a friend of Martin by the name of Darko Vuk, I told him ..." and that's the rest. So just to clarify this, so there would be no confusion for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So you're pointing out that the evidence given yesterday by the witness indicated that she spoke to Drko first, and then to Major Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Dosen, my intention was not to confuse you, rather I was confused by your answer, but perhaps we can move on.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As you were leaving the hospital and in the area where the buses were parked, you said yesterday that there were some other wounded who couldn't walk by themselves. My question hence is the following: When you were returning to the hospital compound, were those wounded still there, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Both yesterday and today in your answers to, I believe, Mr. Borovic, that your first husband was an active officer with the JNA, or professional soldier?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And yesterday you stated that that was one of the reasons how you could tell JNA ranks apart. That's what you claim in your OTP statement, as well as during yesterday's testimony. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Therefore, I conclude that you're familiar with the ranks of the JNA. During your entire stay at the hospital, that is, when you came out of the hospital and when you were searched and when you stood in front of the buses, did you see any other JNA officer being present there?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. No other officer apart from Mr. Sljivancanin next to the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: As you marked yesterday on the photograph, you saw my client next to the first bus, close to the entrance gate at -- of the hospital, and you said that he was wearing a camouflage uniform with the rank of major?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was multi-coloured.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You heard him being addressed as "Major, sir." Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Am I mistaken in thinking that you saw my client's face many times on TV and the newspapers and various other media and that that is how you knew that it was Mr. Sljivancanin?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean after the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, after that, after the events.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I used to see him often, but what you can be certain of is that I spoke with him at the hospital, and that I would claim nothing else if it were not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You only saw my client once you had decided to go and look for help elsewhere because you were not getting any answers as to the fate of the buses. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You approached Mr. Sljivancanin, and you left your daughter Tanja with your husband, who was still in front of the third bus. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Based on all the drawings and the photographs we do have an impression, but could you tell me approximately what was the distance between the place where Mr. Sljivancanin was and the place where Martin was lying on a stretcher?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the distance of, say, the length of a bus, or a bus and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And after the conversation with Mr. Sljivancanin, you returned to your daughter and your husband and Mr. Sljivancanin remained at the place where you had your conversation?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you testified that Mr. Sljivancanin then told two soldiers to lift Martin's stretcher and carry it somewhere. But where to? Did you hear him say anything as regards that? Where was he to be moved to?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear that. I only heard him say that they should carry the stretcher away. That's when I picked up my bag and I followed Martin. Personally I thought he was being taken back to the hospital, but they left him outside in the passage on a stretcher. I didn't hear Mr. Sljivancanin say where he was to be taken to.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will again read a part of your testimony in Dokmanovic case, you testified there under oath, that was page 56, the same day, the 6th of February, 1998. I will read in English again, because that's the official transcript received. [In English] "He looked at me, I turned around and told two soldiers to go back for Martin and to take him back towards the hospital and that we should follow." [Interpretation] Then in 1998, as you've testified, you heard that my client told these soldiers to return your husband to the hospital. Does this refresh your memory in any way as to him moving -- being moved back in front of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not into the hospital, but that they put him back in front of the hospital, exactly where they left him, not inside the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But you heard his words, as you testified then, and today you're saying you didn't?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that I didn't hear Mr. Sljivancanin tell them anything as to where he was to be taken. "Where" can mean a lot of things. He just told them return him in front of the hospital on the stretcher, not into the hospital. I can't tell you exactly where, apart from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But you did hear me read this and that was your statement back then?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That He was to be returned back on the stretcher, and that was in front of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you spoke about your husband's belongings with Sljivancanin, do you remember that at that time you said that you were to carry his stuff? That's what you told my client. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said I had his things and that I wanted him to have them. And then Mr. Sljivancanin said --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So let's not repeat yet again.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but when he asked me who was to carry his stuff, then I said, "Well, all right, I will," in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And after that you put your daughter in front of you and you were pushing her back towards the hospital. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You confirmed to me what you stated then, and that was on the next page of the transcript, and perhaps you can tell me if this is truly so. After the discussion about the belongings, you said the following: [In English] "Then I said if there is no one to carry, then I will carry it. And then I pushed my daughter in front of me and told her to go forward, because I just want to join the other women and children, because my husband kept me -- telling me that we should always be where there are lots of other people, where everybody is together." [Interpretation] Is that the way things went?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did Mr. Sljivancanin tell you to go back to the courtyard or did you do it of your own free will, together with your daughter, as was stated, because your husband kept telling you that you should always stick close to a large group of people?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But Mr. Sljivancanin told me to go and join the other women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your daughter Tanja did not overhear your conversation with Mr. Sljivancanin; isn't that correct? You told her about what you discussed with him?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tanja was crying a lot later, and we spoke about it, and I told her that Mr. Sljivancanin told us to go and join the other women and children. And I don't want to go through all the detail again, but as to whether she was able to overhear the conversation, she may have. It wasn't far away. She could overhear our conversation, but later on we did discuss this between the two of us. She was very close to her father, and she always had many questions as to what had happened. But in any case, she could overhear the conversation. She wasn't too far away.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But to be more precise, you said she could overhear the conversation. But you came back to her after your conversation with Mr. Sljivancanin, and then you went back toward the hospital. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the statement from 1993 consisting of three pages that we saw before the break, nowhere did you mention there that you had any conversation with my client, Mr. Sljivancanin, concerning the belongings. Please take a look at that statement. That is not the statement given to the OTP, but rather the statement with three pages. In that statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that 1993 or 1995, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1993, Your Honour. I apologise for my sloppiness, but that's the statement that was previously on the screen dated the 14th of April, 1993, the statement given to the Ministry of Health. The witness can read out the entire statement, if necessary, but that's what she mentioned there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Dosen, that's the second page from the middle, you can have a look at that. Apart from your discussion with my husband [sic] and saying who was Dosen, a-ha Dosen, apart from that, you never mentioned anything to Mr. Sljivancanin.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter's note that the counsel probably meant "my client."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is correct, sir. It is the statement, but it concerns itself with certain events -- or rather, is unrelated to any testimony. This was more of a general statement about the events one underwent, or rather went through during the war. I only mentioned there that I spoke with Mr. Sljivancanin and we didn't go into any detail. This was simply a statement describing the ordeal I went through. I didn't go into much detail then, particularly not about the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you please answer with a yes or no. In that statement you described your conversation in detail, the conversation you had with that soldier, as well as the event concerning Ruzica Markobasic, then your conversation with Drko, and then the way you were taken out of the hospital, and Capalo's arrival together with the other local paramilitaries. And concerning my client, you only mentioned the dialogue in terms of he asked you what -- which Dosen, oh, that Dosen, and that that's it. Can you confirm that for me?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please answer my next question briefly so as not repeat what we already said. I wanted to tell you that we heard some other witnesses before this Tribunal, some of whom were together with you in the hospital, and some of those people said that my client was not in front of the buses until the very last moment when the buses left. What would you be your comment concerning that?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe they are wrong. And I can say that under oath.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let us follow the chronological order. Now you were moving with Tanja back to the courtyard of the hospital. The trucks you previously described, had they already arrived, or did they come somewhat later, or rather how much time elapsed before the trucks arrived?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Tanja and I returned to the courtyard, two trucks were already there and the wounded were already being placed on the trucks, only the immobile ones, and -- yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you see Martin being loaded on to either of the trucks?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you said that you could see the trucks but not the buses. As I understood it, that was because of the wall of the hospital. Can you tell us whether you saw at least a portion of any of the buses, perhaps the front part, from where you were standing in the courtyard?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I returned to the courtyard, I could see the rear of the first bus, just a small part of the bus. To see them one would have to go further, or lower, spatially put, otherwise you only see but a portion. I could see the trucks much better from where I was than the buses. There were lots of women and children. Perhaps I would have seen the buses had I been anywhere closer or in front of the group, but I went back to my mother-in-law so that I could tell her where Matija [as interpreted], Tadija and Martin were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: May I conclude then that at any given moment you could see a portion of any of the buses as well as the trucks, that they were all there together at the same moment?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that -- for about 10 minutes after I got back, and then afterwards not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm going to remind you once again of your statement from 1985, or rather 1995, the counsel corrects himself. I could perhaps read it out to you. Do you have the statement in front of you, page 8? The third paragraph starting: "By roughly half an hour later."

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 8?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In B/C/S version, in your language, that is.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I seem to have a different document. Just a moment, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] ERN number for the registry is 005374669, I think. [Interpretation] The statement to The Hague Prosecution on the 22nd of August, 1995. Let me just repeat it once again for the registry's representative sitting next to the witness. 00537469. Page 8, number once again 00537476. If you have found it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It starts by a sentence: "Approximately half an hour later."

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and then it goes on Marin Bilic [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, no, hold on a second. Would you please read out that sentence, and that sentence only, very slowly? Can you read the sentence aloud?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "Approximately half an hour later, I saw Marin, Bili, Vidic coming together with a group of observers from the EC and coming in the direction of the group of women and children."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that, when the European Community representatives came along and the fact that he -- that the person accompanying them was Marin Vidic?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You testified yesterday that the representatives of the European Community arrived at around 11.00. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said roughly speaking at 11.00. We didn't have watches. I really can't tell you the exact time. I said that around 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question is very simple. According to what you said in the statement in 1995, and we can agree that our memory is more effective when we talk about short-term rather than long-term memory, so once again, as of the moment when you got there and you saw the buses and trucks, until the moment that the observers of the EC came along about 30 minutes passed, roughly speaking 30 minutes. That's what you said?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, about 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember what the gentleman from the EC and Mr. Vidic did? Who did they talk to?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were talking to the representatives of the army, and they went in towards the hospital. They went inside, because there were more wounded in the hospital, that's when we understood that there were more. And they were going to agree about the convoy and then they could tell the women and children where the convoy would go.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And in your statement in the next sentence you said: "They talked to all of us in general." Do you remember them talking to you?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, afterwards. First of all, they talked among themselves, and they reached agreement, and then they talked to us, and they said that people who wanted to go to Croatia should board certain buses, and people who wanted to go to Belgrade and Novi Sad should board other buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that later on in the convoy when you reached Mitrovica, did they make a list of your names as well, not just the wounded? Do you remember the European observers making a list of the names of all the people in the convoy?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did. They did take our names on a number of occasions. Both on that day when he reached Mitrovica and the following day when we left Sremska Mitrovica, they took our names again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you tell any of them what happened to your husband? Did you show them the medical records that you had on your person?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't talk about it to them. I myself, I mean. I personally did not talk to them about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you show the medical records to my client, the ones that you had, and that referred to your husband?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't show those papers to Mr. Sljivancanin either. I didn't even think of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would just like us to take another look at another document. You have it next to you. It is one of the pieces of evidence from the 65 ter list, it's 703. So it's the form, as far as I can see, the -- from the government of the Republic of Croatia and the commission for the missing and the arrested persons. It is ERN 01006150. Do you have the document in front of you, madam? Thank you. Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what we had to do, what we had to fill out in relation to missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you turn to the last page, please, and can you confirm that your signature is indeed on that page?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If you take a look at this form, did you yourself fill it in? Is this your handwriting or did you dictate it to somebody else?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not my handwriting. The lady who worked at that office filled it in.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you provided her with the relevant data?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us what you understand the term "paramilitaries" to mean? Who would you describe as paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paramilitaries are self-proclaimed soldiers who had not gone through special training, who do not belong -- well, I knew of the JNA, and I did not know of any other type of army back then.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could I put it simpler -- in simpler terms. As far as you were concerned, JNA were not paramilitaries back then; others were, right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I was concerned, JNA was my army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you look at this form once again, page 3. Number 8. Can you see it?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. Yes. In item 8 there is a question in this form: "Who was involved in forceful taking or ferrying away of people?" And you gave the answer: "Members of other paramilitary units." And then in number 9 if he said: "Do you know who did it?" You said: "Yes." And you said that: "There were Vukovar guys wearing uniforms called Capalo and Drko." Now, my question is the following: Who was -- or who is Micko Avramovic.

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Micko Avramovic was a good friend of Martin's.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did he provide you with any information about your husband later on, and if so, what sort of information?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, my Martin took Micko across the Danube in the course of all those events because Micko's daughter was at the hospital in Novi Sad. But they were school friends. And then Micko came to the hospital and he greeted Martin, but he first went in search for his wife, in search of his wife because he didn't know where she was, and he said he would come back to the hospital, and in the meantime all these things happened. And I suppose after the fall of Vukovar he left and went to Germany, and through his mother-in-law, through his wife's mother, he sent me a message, and she was to tell me that he was half an hour late getting to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you also -- did he also tell you in that message that your husband was killed at Negoslavci because Arkan was looking for him because he had known your husband from before? Do you remember that being a part of the message as well?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But he said that he had heard that Martin was supposedly killed by Arkan in Negoslavci. He sent me a message according to which he had heard that and that he was half an hour late getting to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And that's the reason why you mentioned those names in this form, Capalo and Drko, as people who took him away. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I suggest that this document be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, that will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Under the reference 175, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions, but I do have a proposal. That is -- I suppose we should see how we can organise this. All three Defence teams would like to take a look at the original medical records, because we've only seen photocopies, and first of all these photocopies are rather -- rather difficult to read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I would like to give the Prosecution an opportunity to re-examine before 7.00. Can we deal with your proposal at a later time?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite, yes. Definitely, I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mrs. Tuma, do you re-examine?

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Yes, please, Your Honour. Just only one question here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: So perhaps we will have time to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Mrs. Dosen, do you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Is it correct to say that you said both yesterday and today that Serbs from Vukovar left the city before the real conflict began, and also during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: When you were yesterday, and also today, speaking about wells in Vukovar, were people -- where people collected water, did people in Vukovar generally know where those wells were located?

utterances.speaker: LJUBICA DOSEN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether they knew in all of Vukovar, but in the building in which I was, we knew of those houses. We knew that that particular house -- I mean, whenever a house was built in our area, a well would be built as well, so we supposed that almost every house would have a well for the watering of flowers, et cetera, so as not to have -- to use the water supply from the city system, they had these wells.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: Okay, thank you, Mrs. Dosen. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: I'm done so far. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mrs. Tuma. Mrs. Dosen, you will be pleased to know that that is the end of the questions for you. I know it's been a long two days.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: But you will see now that we have come to the end. The Chamber would like to thank you for your assistance in making yourself available for these two days to assist us with your evidence. And you are now free of course to go about your ordinary life. And the court officer there will assist you. So thank you very much, and that concludes our work with you and the need for this videolink.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Lukic, we still have some time. You had a proposition.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to say this in the presence of somebody from the registry who, for example, was sitting next to the witness. The problem is that these photocopies of the medical records that have been submitted to us are not really legible in parts. We know that there are fairly simple systems for coloured photocopies, and I suppose that it is possible to do that in Zagreb, or else that we could perhaps have a scanned coloured photocopy of these documents, or, if possible, for the witness to submit the originals to the representative of the registry so that we can take a look and then we would return them. Let me say straight away that we really do have a problem with the temperature chart, and we can't read anything at all, and you will understand that it's a rather important document from where we stand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mrs. Tuma, can you assist? Is the original the document that has been tendered?

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: The document that we have here with the OTP is the photocopy, and -- but I do have to investigate, because we have some information here that the original has been -- is by the registrar. So -- but I don't know that for to 100 per cent for a fact. So in order to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's quite possible if the witness has given earlier evidence in earlier trials that it is an exhibit in the earlier trial. That may well be where it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may come in at this stage, we heard it from the witness yesterday that she actually had the originals. She said that yesterday. And I seem to see her nodding now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If that is the case, could I ask the court officer who is with her now if it would be possible for him to bring with him back to The Hague the originals for them to be copied more carefully? It seems that that is agreeable, Mr. Lukic. When they come here, perhaps they could just be examined by the Defence at some convenient time, and I think that may be enough for your purposes. But I'm sure that it would be preferable if we could return the originals to Mrs. Dosen as soon as possible. So we will, I expect, be able to assist you, Mr. Lukic. Thank you for that. Is there anything further, Mrs. Tuma?

utterances.speaker: MS. TUMA
utterances.text: No, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm looking at the time, and I think there is no point in thinking of starting a further witness with seven minutes to go, so that we will adjourn now for the evening and resume tomorrow at 2.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 8th day of February, 2006, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.53 p.m.,
